To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intermediate-virulence symbiotic parasites are favored by selection in an environmentally transmitted symbiont infecting a population of susceptible hosts, and that this result holds under a variety of conditions.
natural selection favors the evolution of intermediate virulence in an environmentally-transmitted symbiotic parasite.

the evolution of intermediate virulence is favored by natural selection when (1) parasite transmission rate is an increasing function (of some measure of) virulence, and (2) the parasite is environmentally transmitted and the hosts live in a closed population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of virulence in an environmentally transmited symbiotic parasite infectiung an isolated population of hosts.
the evolution of virulence and the evolution of virulent parasites.
understanding the conditions that favor the co-evolution of intermediate virulence in an environmentally-transmitted parasite.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evolution of intermediate virulence is favored in an isolated population of hosts when the rate of transmission of the parasite increases with the density of susceptible hosts.

the evolution of intermediate virulence is favored by the existence of a positive correlation between host density and the rate of transmission, the existence of a density-dependent mortality rate, the absence of recovery from infection, the absence of a density-dependent birth rate, and the existence of a cost to host reproduction.
the conditions favoring intermediate-virulence are those that lead to an intermediate level of parasite transmission.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conditions that favor the evolutionary emergence of intermediate virulence are the same as those that favor the coexistence of a parasite with its host in the environment.

natural selection for intermediate parasite virulence is a robust property of a broad range of environmentally transmitted parasite-host population models, provided only that the rate of transmission is an increasing, but saturating, function of parasite virulence.

intermediate-virulence is favored by the ecological conditions of (i) a population of finite size, (ii) a low rate of host recovery from infection, (iii) high rates of parasite transmission to hosts, and (iv) low rates of parasite mortality in the environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
natural selection for intermediate-virulence is not a consequence of a trade-off between transmission and growth rate of the parasite.

the evolution of intermediate virulence in environmentally transmitted parasites is a natural consequence of the fact that virulence is costly to the host and the parasite, and that virulence levels that minimize this cost can be expected to evolve in the absence of any special ecological conditions.

intermediate-virulence evolution is a generic feature of environmentally transmitted parasites that act only to reduce host lifespan, and that this result is not dependent on the details of the population dynamics.
